new_statements.rule_in_words: In normal speech the stress accent falls on the initial syllable of the word; the stressed syllable is shortened relative to unstressed ones and is accompanied by a (higher) tone. Sharma adds that accent 'seems' to be significant (potentially contrastive) but his data yield only one pair, rui 'high' (accented) vs rui 'cotton' (unaccented), so a lexically contrastive accent is asserted only tentatively.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the recovered text.
new_statements.exceptions: One putative accentual minimal pair (rui 'high' accented vs rui 'cotton' unaccented) is given as the only evidence for contrastive accent; otherwise 'in a normal speech' initial. Martinez 2021 (pp. 515, 527-9), the modern description, is silent on stress and reports instead a marginal two-way pitch contrast (ràŋ 'horse' vs ráŋ 'mountain') while saying the language is 'not a tonal language from a synchronic perspective'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('in this dialect', 'in a normal speech'), elicited citation forms from the 1980s fieldwork; Sharma's 'accompanied with a tone' means a pitch rise on the stressed syllable, not lexical tone. Sharma treats Chhitkuli as a dialect of Kinnauri and follows the same template as his 1988 Kinnauri grammar ('initial syllable has a higher stress').
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog chit1279 Chhitkul-Rakchham = ISO cik 'Chitkuli Kinnauri'; the same languoid is called 'Chhitkuli dialect' (of Kinnauri) by Sharma 1992, 'Chitkhuli' by Bailey 1920, and 'Chhitkul-Rākchham' by Martinez. Spoken in the two villages Chhitkul and Rakchham, Sangla tahsil, Kinnaur; Sharma's data presumably from Chhitkul village. Distinct from Kinnauri proper (kinn1249), for which Sharma 1988 and Saxena 2022 give their own stress statements.
